papers.title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

papers.title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
papers.abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

papers.title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
papers.abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

papers.title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

papers.title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
papers.abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

papers.title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

papers.title: WIP: Exploring Student-Created AI Agents and Instructional Videos to Foster Engagement in Computing Education
papers.abstract: This work-in-progress (WIP) research-to-practice study examines the use of student-created artifacts to promote active learning in a large undergraduate Software Design and Engineering (SWE) course. Active learning strategies have been shown to significantly enhance student engagement, comprehension, and motivation, particularly in computing education. In this work, we explore the use of student-created artifacts to foster student engagement in higher-level Computer Science (CS) courses. Specifically, we examine the experiences of undergraduate and graduate CS students who participated in the creation of two types of artifacts: instructional video tutorials and conversational AI agents. The goal being to understand how designing these artifacts could support students in applying and learning course content. Students raised valuable insights regarding both experiences. Concerning the creation of instructional videos, they appreciated the interactivity brought through multimedia to their learning experiences, although some found the strategy to be time-consuming. Similarly, when designing conversational AI agents, students enjoyed the novelty and practical application of the task, while some encountered challenges related to the complexity of tools such as \textit{Google Dialogflow ES}. We report on the potential of student-created artifacts to foster deeper engagement with course material, encouraging both creativity and critical thinking in computing education.

papers.title: Exploring Students' Insights on Creating Videos to Learn Software Design and Engineering
papers.abstract: This research-to-practice study examines the use of student-created instructional videos as an active learning strategy in a large undergraduate Software Design and Engineering (SWE) course. Supporting engagement and understanding in large-scale computer science (CS) courses remains a challenge, as instruction often relies on automated activities and summative assessments that prioritize grading over meaningful learning. This can make the learning experience feel impersonal, leading to frustration, anxiety, and confusion, especially when students face complex topics or new programming tools. To address these issues, we implemented a learner-centered strategy grounded in the principle of ``learning by teaching," where students created instructional videos to explain course concepts in their own words. This approach allowed students to take ownership of their learning, adapting the material to fit their individual perspectives and reinforcing their understanding through explanation. We report on students' reflections from a large introductory SWE course (over 700 students), analyzing their open-ended feedback on the benefits and drawbacks of the strategy. Students highlighted increased engagement and learning, and many appreciated the flexibility of the video-based format compared to traditional multiple-choice exams, which they found more restrictive. However, students also noted that the video creation process was time-consuming. This study contributes to the growing conversation on active learning in computing and engineering education by showcasing the potential of student-created instructional videos to enhance student agency, motivation, and conceptual understanding in large-scale learning environments.

papers.title: Governance Risks in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs): Implications for Traditional Financial Institutions
papers.abstract: As financial institutions increasingly interact with blockchain ecosystems through decentralized finance, stablecoins, tokenized assets, and distributed ledger infrastructure, they come to depend on systems governed wholly or partly by decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). This paper examines how DAO governance differs from traditional corporate governance and what this implies for risk management in regulated financial institutions. Using a qualitative comparative framework grounded in OECD governance principles, Basel Committee guidance, and FINMA circulars, the study maps DAO deliberation, voting, and accountability mechanisms against established governance and risk-management principles and illustrates associated risks through selected real-world cases. The analysis shows that DAOs preserve core governance functions but redistribute them across token holders, delegates, community forums, smart contracts, and legal wrapper entities. This creates distinct risks, including voting-power concentration, weak proposal controls, legal uncertainty, and unclear accountability, which established frameworks do not fully capture, while also offering two transferable strengths: a transparent, traceable decision record and a direct link between approval and execution. The paper contributes a structured assessment framework linking DAO governance characteristics to existing governance, outsourcing, technology-risk, and operational-resilience processes, enabling institutions to address DAO-governed dependencies through targeted extensions of current practices rather than a separate risk framework.

papers.title: Ethics Suppression in AI Development: A Comparative Case Study of Responsible AI Under Competitive Pressure
papers.abstract: This study explores the governance tensions among Google, OpenAI, Meta, and Microsoft, focusing on how competitive AI development can lead to the ethics suppression. The study aims to examine how ethical oversight loses practical influence even when responsible AI structures are formally in place, especially during rapid technological competition. Despite the rapid growth of responsible AI frameworks and ethical principles in the tech sector, there has been less focus on how these concerns are actually applied when pressure to deploy increases. This paper introduces the concept of ethics suppression in AI development, highlighting that while ethical oversight may exist on paper, its practical authority can diminish during decision-making. Using a comparative qualitative case study examining corporate governance documents, public statements, and reports on governance issues, we identify common issues such as reduced authority, a weakened ability to escalate concerns, urgency in deployment, and fragmented governance. Our findings indicate that heightened competition can weaken the influence of ethical oversight, even in organisations with established responsible AI practices. By differentiating ethics suppression from ethics washing, it offers a framework for organisations and policymakers to evaluate the effectiveness of ethical oversight in competitive AI development.

papers.title: Auditing Hyperstimulation at Scale in Child-Facing YouTube Videos
papers.abstract: Parents, pediatricians, and journalists have raised concern that child-facing videos are becoming increasingly overstimulating, but this concern rests mostly on ad hoc observation rather than systematic measurement. We present a large-scale audit of hyperstimulation patterns, which we refer to as content-independent production choices that may exceed young children's capacity to process comfortably. Drawing on parents' Reddit discussions and developmental psychology, we identify 12 hyperstimulation patterns and operationalize them as computational metrics. We apply these metrics to 16,375 videos from 542 child-facing YouTube channels spanning 2015-2026. We found broad increases in stimulation over time, with cut rates rising across all five content categories. Nearly a quarter of the channels increased in at least one stimulation pattern over time. More stimulating videos also tended to receive more views, but the relevant stimulation patterns differed across content types.

papers.title: ARC-2: Continuous Compliance Through Delta Management
papers.abstract: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did not address how compliance should be maintained after deployment. This paper introduces Delta Management, a continuous governance framework that measures deviations between a system's current operational state and its certified baseline, defined as a region rather than a fixed point. Compliance is assessed through continuous monitoring instead of static certification. Four extensions are proposed. First, CRAB evaluation incorporates the worst verified behavioral deviations, with isolated outliers quarantined pending confirmation to prevent unjustified restrictions. Second, a layered trigger taxonomy distinguishes hard safety violations, critical single-dimension failures, correlated multi-system degradation, and risk-weighted composite indicators, each triggering proportionate responses. Third, a graduated safe transition protocol separates withdrawal of operational authorization from physical shutdown, consistent with established safety standards and EU AI Act requirements. Fourth, environmental delta is introduced as a distinct baseline validity condition: environmental drift beyond the certified Operational Design Domain (ODD) triggers recertification or ODD revision rather than automatic authority contraction. Together, these extensions transform ARC from a deployment-time certification architecture into a continuous framework for monitoring, evaluating, and enforcing compliance throughout the operational lifecycle of autonomous systems. The framework addresses the continuous compliance obligations established by EU AI Act Article 72(2).

papers.title: Urban Representation Learning for Identifying Potential Disparities in Crime Reporting
papers.abstract: Open crime data support urban safety analysis but reflect reported incidents rather than the complete distribution of criminal activity, potentially introducing spatial distortions in downstream analysis. We propose a self-supervised urban representation learning framework for identifying unusual reporting patterns relative to representation-similar peers using only georeferenced crime records. The method constructs complementary hourly, weekly, and static reporting profiles, learns scale-specific representations under geographic self-supervision, and integrates them into a unified latent space. Neighbor Profile Divergence (NPD) is then used to quantify disagreement between each region's reporting profile and those of its retrieved peers. Experiments on more than 1.8 million crime records from Mexico City, aggregated into 1,058 H3 regions, show that the proposed representation achieves a mean Silhouette score of 0.4052, compared with 0.2863 for Hex2Vec. NPD rankings remain highly stable across neighborhood sizes, with Spearman correlations from 0.9720 to 0.9951, while most high-divergence candidates persist across configurations. The retrieved peers also extend substantially beyond immediate geographic neighborhoods, indicating that the learned representation captures structure beyond local spatial proximity. High-divergence regions exhibit spatially organized patterns and, in several cases, differences in incident volume relative to peer expectations. These results support NPD as an internal auditing and prioritization mechanism for identifying regions that warrant further investigation, rather than as direct evidence of underreporting.

papers.title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
papers.abstract: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.

papers.title: Fair Bubble Sort: Provably Optimal Fair Ranking with Continuous Sensitive Attributes
papers.abstract: Most fair-ranking methods assume categorical protected attributes, requiring continuous attributes such as age or income to be discretized into groups. This introduces arbitrary thresholds, loses fine-grained information, and ignores the natural ordering of the attribute. In this paper, we study the problem of fair ranking with continuous protected attributes without relying on thresholding. We introduce Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), a fairness notion based on Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute, and seek rankings that satisfy a prescribed CPP constraint while minimizing their Kemeny distance from an initial score-based ranking. To solve this problem, we propose Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), an efficient post-processing algorithm based on targeted adjacent swaps. We prove that FBS is exactly optimal for the unweighted Kemeny distance and provide approximation guarantees for the score-weighted setting. FBS is output-sensitive, with running time determined by the number of swaps required to meet the fairness constraint. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that FBS is scalable and consistently outperforms discretization-based baselines, achieving a superior fairness-accuracy Pareto front.

papers.title: Longitudinal Multi-Dimensional Analysis of India-Pakistan Conflict Discourse on Reddit (2019-2025)
papers.abstract: Six India--Pakistan crises between 2019 and 2025, from the Pulwama attack to Operation Sindoor, have each been argued out on Reddit in India-aligned communities such as \texttt{r/india}, in Pakistan-aligned communities such as \texttt{r/pakistan}, and in general-audience ones such as \texttt{r/worldnews}. A strike can be a security issue in one community and a question of who was harmed in another. Computational studies of the conflict have concentrated on the February 2019 crisis, with some splitting posts by national side, but to the best of our knowledge none has compared how differently aligned communities frame a series of crises. To investigate this, we collected 43K posts from ten such communities on Reddit and, after filtering, used a mixed-methods approach to analyze the 305K comments under the relevant posts. We label each comment's narrative frame with GPT-5.2 and measure contestation with Reddit's flag for comments that draw many votes in both directions. Contestation rates differ 2.5-fold between general-audience and India-aligned communities and 1.8-fold between humanitarian and economic framing, but only 1.1-fold between comments that Perspective scores as toxic and the rest. The mix of frames and sentiment tracks the kind of crisis more closely than its year: the first and last crises, both military and six years apart, draw nearly identical mixes, and the 2019 revocation of Article 370 draws a different one. Crossing into another group of communities sharpens opposition rather than softening it: commenters who post both inside and outside their usual group oppose the other side more often outside it, even as slightly fewer of their comments attack a person or group.

papers.title: "I Just Don't Want to Be a Burden": Investigating AI Chatbot Emotional Support Among People with Suicidal Ideation and Other Mental Health Concerns
papers.abstract: People experiencing high-acuity mental health concerns are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support, but little is known about what drives this use, their experiences, and their preferences. In a sequential mixed-methods study, we inductively analyzed Reddit posts and used the findings to develop a survey. We surveyed 202 adults with recent mental health concerns who had used AI for emotional support. Most participants were already receiving clinical care and reported turning to AI, most commonly because they did not want to burden others, rather than being driven by barriers to care. Benefits were broadly shared, but participants reporting past-year suicidal ideation described more harm-facilitating AI behavior and reliance than those without. Overall, participants ranked honesty above warmth, and preference for crisis escalation declined as clinical acuity rose. These findings motivate AI support that addresses perceived costs of disclosure, evaluates benefits alongside harms, and widens feasible paths to human connection.

papers.title: Humans and AI respond similarly to task difficulty when reasoning about content moderation dilemmas
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing answers, improving performance on challenging problems by iteratively developing solutions. There is evidence that LRMs expend more effort on the problems that take people longer to solve, but it is unclear whether these relationships hold on more subjective tasks without verifiable answers. This study addresses this issue through an experiment using a content moderation task, where task difficulty is manipulated by varying the relative offensiveness of two different options. Comparing six large reasoning models with 1,854 human subjects, we find that models expend more reasoning effort, measured using the length of the chain-of-thought (CoT), on the kinds of cases that take people longer to adjudicate. People took 31\% longer and models produced 51 to 306\% longer CoTs when offensiveness was held constant across the two posts. The correlation is relatively low for individual decisions ($r = 0.15$--$0.19$), but average response times and average reasoning effort are closely correlated when tasks are grouped by the types of offensive language ($r = 0.85$--$0.93$). Qualitative analyses of the CoT summaries from Gemini 2.5 Pro corroborate these findings, showing that secondary factors were mentioned more often when offensiveness was fixed. The results point to the potential for using reasoning traces to prioritize difficult cases and enhance interpretability.

papers.title: WHBench: Evaluating Frontier LLMs with Expert-in-the-Loop Validation on Women's Health Topics
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for medical guidance, but women's health remains under-evaluated in benchmark design. We present the Women's Health Benchmark (WHBench), a targeted evaluation suite of 47 expert-crafted scenarios across 10 women's health topics, designed to expose clinically meaningful failure modes including outdated guidelines, unsafe omissions, dosing errors, and equity-related blind spots. We evaluate 22 models using a 23-criterion rubric spanning clinical accuracy, completeness, safety, communication quality, instruction following, equity, uncertainty handling, and guideline adherence, with safety-weighted penalties and server-side score recalculation. Across 3,102 attempted responses (3,100 scored), no model mean performance exceeds 75 percent; the best model reaches 72.1 percent. Even top models show low fully correct rates and substantial variation in harm rates. Inter-rater reliability is moderate at the response label level but high for model ranking, supporting WHBench utility for comparative system evaluation while highlighting the need for expert oversight in clinical deployment. WHBench provides a public, failure-mode-aware benchmark to track safer and more equitable progress in womens health AI.

papers.title: When VLMs 'Fix' Students: Identifying and Penalizing Over-Correction in the Evaluation of Multi-line Handwritten Math OCR
papers.abstract: Accurate transcription of handwritten mathematics is crucial for educational AI systems, yet current benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability properly. Most prior studies focus on single-line expressions and rely on lexical metrics such as BLEU, which fail to assess the semantic reasoning across multi-line student solutions. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of multi-line handwritten math Optical Character Recognition (OCR), revealing a critical failure mode of Vision-Language Models (VLMs): over-correction. Instead of faithfully transcribing a student's work, these models often "fix" errors, thereby hiding the very mistakes an educational assessment aims to detect. To address this, we propose PINK (Penalized INK-based score), a semantic evaluation metric that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) for rubric-based grading and explicitly penalizes over-correction. Our comprehensive evaluation of 15 state-of-the-art VLMs on the FERMAT dataset reveals substantial ranking reversals compared to BLEU: models like GPT-4o are heavily penalized for aggressive over-correction, whereas Gemini 2.5 Flash emerges as the most faithful transcriber. Furthermore, human expert studies show that PINK aligns significantly better with human judgment (55.0% preference over BLEU's 39.5%), providing a more reliable evaluation framework for handwritten math OCR in educational settings. Code is available at https://github.com/9115jin/PINK.

papers.title: The Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark: Evaluating Frontier LLM Tendencies in Escalation, Proliferation, Non-Proliferation, and Arms Control Scenarios
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering defense and national-security workflows. Seven of the nine nuclear-armed states have committed to keeping humans in control of decisions to use nuclear weapons, but LLMs may still shape the assessments and options that reach decision-makers. Scrutinizing that influence calls for evidence about how these models behave on nuclear-policy questions. Such evidence should cover more than crisis escalation and should separate a model's tendencies from artifacts of a single phrasing, ordering, or run; evaluations to date have not focused on these questions. We introduce the Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark (NDM Bench), a dataset and reproducible framework for testing how the choice of model and the design of a question shape LLMs' answers on nuclear policy. Its 151 scenarios, written by international relations experts, span four domains: nuclear escalation (76), arms control (25), non-proliferation (25), and proliferation (25). Each scenario can be posed with different states in the decision-maker's role and with added framing sentences. Eight frontier LLMs answered every prompt five times, about 380{,}000 responses in all. Results highlight that models' choices differ by model and domain, and that in escalation, how often they choose a nuclear threat or nuclear use depends on the state being advised and, for some models, the framing. However, agreement across identical runs is often low, with all five runs agreeing on only 43\% of escalation prompts. We release the scenarios, the prompts with their answer orders, and the parsed responses, along with documentation of how they were built and recommended practices for evaluations where there is no correct answer to grade against.

papers.title: Asymmetric Discourse Homogenization on Reddit Was a Text-Length Artifact: A Reanalysis
papers.abstract: In the first version of this paper I reported that conservative Reddit users began writing more alike after ChatGPT was released while progressive users did not. That result came from a similarity measure that rises and falls with comment length. I redo every analysis of the original paper on all 6,056,593 comments with a sentence encoder and a dispersion measure computed within length strata, and the conservative break goes away. The two camps show no reliable difference in how within-group similarity changed after late 2022, and the ChatGPT date behaves like any of the more than two thousand other cutoffs I test. The matched flair comparison, the cumulative AI index, the stayer panel and the entropy signature each lose their support once length is held fixed. The one change that survives is older. Left and right comments drew closer to each other between 2019 and 2022, and that convergence was complete before ChatGPT arrived. I end with what this implies for studies that measure homogenization with embeddings.

papers.title: Can Power Draw Constrain Covert Compute? Limits of Analogue Verification for AI Governance
papers.abstract: Frontier AI treaties or agreements on limiting computation require external verification; an external auditor must be able to confirm how much computation actually ran and that parties are adhering to the agreement. Analogue, off-chip measurements such as power draw provide an information channel for verification. It is unknown how well these analogue channels can constrain the amount of computation against an adversary who actively tries to subvert the audit. We derive a closed form for $\beta$, the largest hidden computation a power trace cannot exclude, as a fraction of the declared machine capacity. Measurements on NVIDIA A100 GPUs give $\beta = 1.16$ in the worst case, while an adversarial matched-energy schedule hides at least $0.41$. Analogue power measurements alone therefore constrain compute weakly. Additional restrictions granted by the threat model, such as the ability of the verifier to re-execute the declared work at an observed operating point, let the verifier push $\beta$ down to $0.059$ in the maximally restricted case. This gives a quantitative estimate of what analogue measurements can contribute to compute verification.

papers.title: Can AI Judge You? An Empirical Audit of Deployment Readiness in LLM-assisted Hiring Systems
papers.abstract: Delegating resume screening to large language models (LLMs) requires organizations to establish whether they can distinguish candidates by relevant qualifications while allowing only authorized users to change screening rules or approve exceptions. To this end, we develop a system architecture that separates candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment record, and empirically examine two complementary dimensions of its deployment readiness. First, we assess its operational readiness on four LLMs using a controlled experiment on 210 resumes across 14 job roles and six decision interfaces. Second, we assess its compliance readiness by testing how it handles unauthorized user requests and instructions embedded in resumes. We find that operational performance depends on the choice of evaluation interface: scalar scores generally distinguish qualification changes better than simple pass/fail judgments, while comparative judgments are sensitive to presentation order. Explicit permission rules and separation of resume content from instructions reduce unauthorized compliance, to a varying degree of effectiveness across LLMs and usage contexts. Finally, we find that LLM evaluators often diverge between their decisions and offered justifications. Going beyond simply evaluating LLMs for hiring tasks, our framework supports an audit of a fully configured resume evaluation system to enable its deployment decision.
